title: The Orator's Treasure-House
description: What Rome wanted from memory, Quintilian's walk through a house, and his doubts
tryIt: Give each of tomorrow's five main jobs a symbol in Quintilian's style, place them through your home from the front door inwards, and walk the house in your head before breakfast.

concepts.title: How it works: the speaker's treasure-house
concepts.contentHtml:
Picture yourself in Rome, about to speak in a crowded court. No notes, no screen, no prompter: everything you plan to say has to be in your head, in order, and ready to come out under pressure. For the people who first wrote the art of memory down, that was the whole point of it.

The Rhetorica ad Herennium, the Roman handbook you met in Your First Palace, was written for rhetoric students who gathered around their teacher circa 86–82 BC,1 as the historian Frances Yates dated it. Its author turns to memory as "the treasure-house of the ideas supplied by Invention2" and the guardian of all the parts of rhetoric. He splits it in two. Natural memory is the one you were born with. Artificial memory is the one strengthened by a kind of training and system of discipline,3 and the art of memory was that training.

Later the teacher Quintilian gave memory a chapter in the eleventh book of his Institutio Oratoria, a complete course for training an orator. He opened with the same image: it is not without good reason, he wrote, that memory has been called the treasure-house of eloquence.4 Memory brings before the speaker the store of precedents, laws, rulings, sayings and facts that he must hold ready for immediate use.

What did a trained memory look like? Yates gathered the feats that impressed the ancients. The elder Seneca, a teacher of rhetoric, could repeat two thousand names in the order in which they had been given.5 When a class of two hundred or more students each spoke a line of poetry, he could recite all the lines in reverse order, from the last back to the first. Augustine, also trained in rhetoric, told of a friend called Simplicius who could recite Virgil backwards.6

Backwards is the clue. A list learned by rote runs one way, like a song. A list stored on places can be walked in either direction, and Yates suggests the artificial memory may explain these feats.7 Notice what Rome admired: not a bigger memory, but order on demand.

concepts.title: Drill: Quintilian's house
concepts.contentHtml:
Quintilian gives the clearest walk through the method to survive from Rome. Choose a place as large and varied as possible, he says, such as a spacious house divided into a number of rooms.1 Give each point a symbol: something from navigation, such as an anchor, or from warfare, such as a weapon.2 Then set the symbols in order. The first thought is placed, as it were, in the forecourt; the second, let us say, in the living-room;3 the rest go in due order all round the impluvium, the light-well in the center of the hall with a cistern beneath to catch rainwater,4 and on into bedrooms and parlors, even into the care of statues. To speak, you visit the places in turn and demand back each deposit from its custodian.

  1. Build the house. Use the plan above, or a real house you know well: eight stations, in order.
  2. Make a symbol for each point. One object per idea, the way Quintilian's anchor stands for ships.
  3. Place them in order, one per station, and give each symbol something to do in its room.
  4. Walk and collect. Stroll through and ask each place for its deposit.
  5. Walk back out. Recite the points from the dining room to the forecourt, the way the elder Seneca ran his lists in reverse.
Drill You are a senator with eight points to make. Give each a symbol, place them on the eight stations in order, then walk the house both ways. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. the grain fleet (an anchor)
  2. the frontier war (a spear)
  3. the new aqueduct
  4. the price of bread
  5. the chariot races
  6. road repairs
  7. a temple fire
  8. the coming election

The house need not be a house, or even real. What works in a house, Quintilian adds, works just as well with public buildings, a long journey, the ramparts of a city, or even pictures,5 and we may even imagine such places for ourselves.

concepts.title: Myth check: word for word?
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Roman orators used the memory palace to learn every speech word for word.
Reality Quintilian, the most practical of the Roman teachers, thought the places were best for lists, such as a number of names in the order in which you heard them. He mentions people who, after an auction, could state what they had sold to each buyer,1 a feat alleged of the orator Hortensius. But the method, he says, will be of less service in learning the various parts of a set speech,2 because thoughts do not call up the same images as material things. His own advice is plainer. Learn a long speech piecemeal, in sections that are not too short.3 Learn a passage from the same tablets on which you wrote it,4 so that the mind's eye follows the lines. Above all, learn much by heart and think much, if possible daily.5 He even noticed the effect of sleep: the interval of a single night, he wrote, will greatly increase the strength of the memory.6

Wait, really? Quintilian was a skeptic about the superstars. Metrodorus of Scepsis was said to have found 360 places in the twelve signs of the zodiac,7 and Quintilian put it down to vanity and boastfulness.8 He passes on the stories that Cyrus knew the name of every soldier in his army and that Themistocles spoke excellent Persian after a year's study, but with a careful "is believed" and "is said". Of people who could repeat any number of verses after one hearing, he admits he never had the good fortune to be present at such a performance.9 The method was real; the legends around it grew in the telling.

title: Memory for the Soul
description: How medieval scholars made the art a virtue, Aquinas's four rules and Llull's wheels
tryIt: Pick four ideas you want to live by this week, give each an unusual image, set them in order along your route to work, and run through them each evening, as Aquinas advised.

concepts.title: How it works: from the law court to the cloister
concepts.contentHtml:
You might expect a Roman speaker's trick to fade along with Rome. Instead the art of memory found a new and grander job in the Middle Ages: it became part of being good.

The route ran through a mistake. Medieval readers believed Cicero had written the Ad Herennium. His early work De inventione circulated as the "First Rhetoric" and was immediately followed by the Ad Herennium as the "Second Rhetoric",1 and the pair still traveled together when the first printed edition appeared at Venice in 1470.2 That mattered, because at the end of the First Rhetoric Cicero names the parts of3 prudence: memory, intelligence and foresight. If memory was part of a cardinal virtue, then the "Tullian" art of training it was a moral matter.

That is why the Dominican scholars Albertus Magnus and Thomas Aquinas treated the places and images of "Tullius" as, in Yates's words, a moral and religious duty.4 Aquinas wrote his method into the Summa Theologiae, under the question whether memory is a part of prudence: there are four things, he says, whereby a man perfects his memory.5 You will use them in the drill.

Books existed, of course, but they did not replace memory. The literary historian Mary Carruthers argues in The Book of Memory (1990) that medieval culture was fundamentally memorial.6 For the Middle Ages, the book was itself a memory aid and only one way to keep a text in mind.7 Memory was central to composition and conversation, and a foundation of character, judgment, citizenship and piety.8 Think of the difference between owning a book and knowing it: only the second lets you turn a text over in your mind while you walk, pray or write.

concepts.title: Drill: Aquinas's rules, Llull's letters
concepts.contentHtml:
Aquinas's four rules read like a modern coaching sheet. First, take some suitable yet somewhat unwonted, that is unusual, illustration of the thing, since the unwonted strikes us more.1 Second, carefully consider and set in order what you want to keep, so that you may pass easily from one memory to another.2 Third, be anxious and earnest about it: the more a thing is impressed on the mind, the less it slips.3 Fourth, reflect on it often.

Now meet a medieval art with no rooms at all. Ramon Llull of Majorca lived from 1232 to 1316.4 He conceived his Ars, or Art, as a system for finding truth, an instrument for interfaith debate aimed at winning converts.5 Its later form runs on an alphabet of nine letters, B to K,6 each standing for a divine attribute he called a Dignity, and its figures turn. In the most famous, an outer circle inscribed B to K stays still while circles inscribed the same way revolve inside it,7 so you can read off combinations: BC can mean "goodness is great".8 To work the Art in your head, you need the alphabet cold.

  1. Make it unusual. One strange, concrete picture per Dignity: greatness as a giant stepping over a cathedral.
  2. Set it in order. Put the nine pictures on nine places along a route, B first.
  3. Care about it. Tie each picture to someone or something that matters to you.
  4. Reflect often. Run through the nine tonight and again tomorrow.
  5. Turn the wheel. Pick any two letters, say B and F, and speak the sentence they make: goodness is wise.
Drill Learn Llull's nine letters and what each stands for, in order, using Aquinas's rules. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. B goodness
  2. C greatness
  3. D duration
  4. E power
  5. F wisdom
  6. G will
  7. H virtue
  8. I truth
  9. K glory

concepts.title: Myth check: rote and rare books
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Medieval people memorized because books were scarce, and memorizing meant parroting.
Reality Carruthers's work turns both halves around. Books were themselves treated as memory aids, and a trained memory was where a medieval writer composed and judged, not merely where he stored. Aquinas's rules are about meaning, order and care, not repetition alone. And Llull's wheels did not store anything: they generated new combinations of ideas. Yates contrasts the two medieval arts neatly. Llull, she writes, introduces movement into memory;1 of the static art of places and his turning letters, the first art is the more artistic, but the second is the more scientific.2

Wait, really? Preachers built memory images that were never meant to be painted. Yates describes one of Idolatry from Ridevall's Fulgentius metaforalis, a handbook designed for the use of preachers.3 The figure is shown as blind and deaf, because idolatry springs from flattery, which blinds and deafens its objects.4 She is proclaimed as a criminal; she has a sad and disfigured face, because one cause of idolatry is inordinate grief; and she is diseased, because idolatry is a kind of unregulated love. Each feature carries one point of the sermon, and a short Latin verse sums up the whole figure. Yates concluded it was designed to stir memory by its strikingness, not intended to be represented save invisibly in memory:5 a picture you carry, not one you hang.

title: Theaters and Wheels
description: Camillo's walk-in theater, Bruno's wheel of inventors and the printing myth
tryIt: Turn seven rooms or corners you pass every day into a seven-gate theater, put this week's seven tasks there as people holding objects, and read them back from the doorway.

concepts.title: How it works: a theater for the mind
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1532 Viglius Zuichemus, then in Padua, wrote to Erasmus that everyone was talking about a certain Giulio Camillo,1 who was said to have built an amphitheater, a work of wonderful skill. Then Viglius went to Venice and was let inside.

"The work is of wood, marked with many images, and full of little boxes,2" he reported. Camillo stammered badly,3 showed him a mass of papers drawn from Cicero, and called the theater by many names: now a built or constructed mind and soul, now a windowed one.4 Yates judged it a building large enough to be entered by at least two people at once,5 since the two men were in it together. Camillo, born about 1480, had already been to France in 1530, where King Francis I gave him money towards the work.6 Near the end of his life he dictated an outline over seven mornings,7 and after his death it was published in 15508 as L'Idea del Theatro.

From that little book Yates reconstructed the plan. The theater rises in seven grades or steps, divided by seven gangways representing the seven planets.9 Camillo reversed the normal theater: there is no audience, and the solitary spectator stands where the stage would be,10 gazing at images on seven times seven gates. And since in ancient theaters the most distinguished people sat lowest, the most important things sit in the lowest grade.11

Notice the ambition. Quintilian's house held one speech. Camillo claimed that all things the human mind can conceive could be expressed in his theater by bodily signs,12 so that the beholder takes them in at a glance. The art of memory was turning into an art of organizing knowledge.

concepts.title: Drill: Bruno's wheel of inventors
concepts.contentHtml:
Fifty years after Camillo's theater caused its stir, the art reached the French court through Giordano Bruno. Bruno later told the Venetian Inquisitors that King Henri III had summoned him to ask whether his memory was natural or came from magic. "I proved to him that it was not obtained by magic art but by science,1" he said, and he then printed a book on memory, De umbris idearum (On the Shadows of the Ideas, 1582),2 dedicated to the king.

Its pages repeat the figure of a circle marked with thirty letters,3 sometimes drawn as concentric wheels, and Yates notes that no Parisian could have failed to recognize them as Llull's combinatory wheels.4 Bruno was fusing Llull's turning letters with the classical places and images. On the outermost wheels of one system he inscribed a list of 150 items,5 a procession of inventors: Erichtonius with the chariot, Pyrodes drawing fire from flint, Isis who first ordered gardens,6 and on through the history of human skill. Every entry is a person joined to a thing, which is exactly the kind of image that sticks.

  1. Make seven gates. Seven rooms, doors or corners you know, in a fixed order like Camillo's gangways, plus the threshold as you leave.
  2. Cast the person. See each inventor as a vivid figure: a goddess in a helmet, a smith black with soot.
  3. Put the thing in their hands. The invention is held, used or shown off, never just lying nearby.
  4. One pair per place, in order, with the eighth on the threshold.
  5. Turn the wheel. Walk the gates naming each pair, then start at the fourth gate and go round.
Drill Eight pairs from Bruno's wheel, in the order Yates gives them. Place each inventor holding the invention, one per gate. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. Erichtonius: the chariot
  2. Pyrodes: fire from flint
  3. Isis: gardens
  4. Minerva: oil
  5. Aristeus: honey
  6. Doxius: building with clay
  7. Talus: the saw
  8. Choraebus: pottery

concepts.title: Myth check: did printing kill it?
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth Once books could be printed, nobody needed to memorize, and the art of memory died.
Reality Printing gave the art its biggest audience. The first printed memory treatise appeared at Venice in 1482,1 as an appendix to a book on rhetoric by Jacobus Publicius. Peter of Ravenna's Phoenix (1491) became the most universally known of all the memory textbooks,2 reprinted in Bologna, Cologne, Venice and Vienna and translated into English around 1548;3 Yates credits its success to bringing the art out into the lay world.4 The German Dominican Johannes Romberch,5 in his Congestorium artificiose memorie (1520), printed visual alphabets,6 with compasses or a ladder for A and a hoe for N.7 Yates put the puzzle herself: printing seemed to have made the great medieval memories unnecessary,8 so why the fresh surge of interest in the strange systems of Camillo, Bruno and Robert Fludd?

Fludd printed his memory theater in 1619, in a vast history of the two worlds, the universe and man, and Yates even argued that it could throw light on Shakespeare's Globe Theatre.9 Printing did not end the art; it changed what people wanted from it.

Wait, really? The art of memory may have cost Bruno his life. A Venetian gentleman, Giovanni Mocenigo, wrote inviting him to teach him the art of memory, and it was Mocenigo who denounced him to the Inquisition.10 The art of memory, Yates concluded, is at the very center of the life and death of Bruno.11 At dawn on 17 February 1600 he was led out to the Campo de' Fiori12 in Rome and burned alive.

title: Palaces Abroad, Images on Trial
description: Ricci's palace in Ming China, the Puritan attack on images and Yates's rediscovery
tryIt: Rewrite one page of notes as an outline running from the most general heading down to the details, recall it from the outline alone, then try the same page as images in your palace and compare.

concepts.title: How it works: a palace for the examinations
concepts.contentHtml:
Imagine a country where children spend long hours memorizing texts from the age of three,1 and official posts go to those who pass the civil examinations. Now imagine you are a foreigner who says he knows a better way to remember. That was the Jesuit Matteo Ricci (1552–1610)2 in Ming China.

In a letter from Nanchang dated 4 November 1595, Ricci says he had started to teach the "memory of places" to some of his visitors.3 Word spread that the foreigner had a prodigious memory, and the governor of Jiangxi province invited him to teach his techniques to his three sons, then preparing for the civil examinations.4 The scholars of the city, Ricci wrote, soon learned that he knew an art of memory, something unprecedented for them.5

The result was a short book in Chinese, Xiguo Jifa (The Western Art of Memory, 1596). Its first chapter treats memory as a storehouse;6 its second retells Cicero's story of how Simonides created the method;7 the rest explains places and images. Ricci's own twist was to use Chinese characters as the images, analyzing how each is built so that it could stand in a palace.8 The historian Ana Carolina Hosne doubts it worked for Chinese readers. A character already gives more direct access to its meaning than a word in an alphabet,9 and Ricci seems to have ignored local memory aids,10 such as the diagrams Chinese scholars used to support textual study.

The Jesuits did not always insist on their own methods. In Peru, Hosne notes, they allowed and even encouraged the pre-Hispanic quipus, knotted-string devices, for memorizing Christian doctrine and for confession.11

concepts.title: Drill: Perkins against the images
concepts.contentHtml:
While Ricci built palaces in China, the art was on trial in England. Early in 1584 the Scot Alexander Dicson1 published a memory treatise in the style of Bruno. A Cambridge author who signed himself "G.P." answered with the Antidicsonus and a tract bound with it against "the impious artificial memory of Dicson".2 Yates argued that G.P. was the Puritan divine and Cambridge Ramist William Perkins.3 Against Dicson's images he urged the dialectical order of the reformer Petrus Ramus as the only right and moral way of memorizing,4 and he mocked Dicson as a "Scepsian", after Metrodorus of Scepsis and his zodiac. Dicson took the insult as a badge and replied under the pen name Heius Scepsius.5 The quarrel, Yates concluded, was at bottom a religious controversy:6 Ramus had read the Old Testament ban on graven images as applying to the art's vivid pictures too.7

The Ramist method has two moves: structure a subject from its most general concepts down to the most specific, then memorize it by repetition.8 The order is the memory. Try it, then judge for yourself.

  1. Find the most general heading. For the drill: musical instruments.
  2. Divide it. Strings and winds.
  3. Divide again. Bowed and plucked; brass and woodwind.
  4. Recite the outline from the top, branch by branch, until it runs without a pause.
  5. Race Dicson. Tomorrow, recall the eight. Then learn a list of your own as images in your palace and compare.
Drill Learn these eight the Ramist way, as an outline read from top to bottom. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. violin
  2. cello
  3. harp
  4. lute
  5. trumpet
  6. horn
  7. flute
  8. oboe

concepts.title: Myth check: it died because it failed
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth The art of memory faded because people found out that it did not work.
Reality Nobody tested it and found it wanting; it lost an argument. In the England of 1583, Yates writes, Protestant educational authorities were against the art.1 Erasmus did not encourage it, Melanchthon had banished it from rhetoric,2 and for the Puritan Ramists the imageless "dialectical order" was the only art of memory.3 When psychologists finally did test the method of loci, centuries later, it worked, as you saw in Your First Palace.

The story itself was half forgotten until Frances Yates of the Warburg Institute pieced it together. Her interest began with Bruno: a memory system excavated from his Shadows was first displayed in a lecture at the Warburg Institute in May 1952,4 and the plan of Camillo's theater in January 1955.5 The result, The Art of Memory (1966), set out the story this skill has followed.

It is not the last word. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy says attempts like Yates's to make magic or memory techniques the key to Bruno's thought remain valuable for their details and insights, but that they obscure Bruno's stated intention to articulate a new philosophy.6

Wait, really? Dicson's book outlived the quarrel. It was reprinted in 1597 by Thomas Basson, an English printer settled at Leiden,7 under a new title: Thamus, the name of the Egyptian king in Plato who warned that writing would weaken memory. You will meet him in the next lesson.

title: Memory Without Writing
description: Homer's singers, the Vedic recitation patterns, songlines and Plato's worry about writing
tryIt: Learn a short verse of a poem or song in krama style, saying each pair of neighboring words aloud, then recite the whole verse from memory tomorrow.

concepts.title: How it works: singers who compose as they sing
concepts.contentHtml:
In the summer of 1933 Milman Parry, a professor of classics at Harvard, went to Yugoslavia to test his ideas about how the Iliad and Odyssey were composed. You may have met his stock phrases, such as "swift-footed Achilles", in the literature topics. What he wanted now was living evidence. From June 1934 to September 1935 he returned with Albert Lord and the singer Nikola Vujnović, and in those 15 months they collected over 12,500 texts. Many were recorded on aluminum discs, using two turntables joined by a switch, so a singer could go on without interruption. The recordings fill over 3,500 discs.

What did they show? Lord set it out in The Singer of Tales (1960). The singers were not reciting a fixed text. An oral poem, he wrote, is not composed for but in performance,1 and every performance is a separate song.2 Versions of the same song by the same singer differed, most of all in their endings, because the end of a song is sung less often.3 Tradition survived by what Lord called the constant re-creation of it.4

Other traditions aim at the opposite. In Australia, Aboriginal songlines carry Law, rights and responsibilities, land use, and astronomical and navigation knowledge. A 2021 study co-written by Tyson Yunkaporta, a member of the Apalech clan of Western Cape York, describes these stories as ancient, showing little variation over long periods of time, and carefully learned and guarded by the Elders who are their custodians. They can be expressed in song, dance, painting and rock art. Some of what they hold is restricted, and it is not ours to learn; this course stays with what custodians share publicly.

concepts.title: Drill: the Vedic patterns
concepts.contentHtml:
The Vedas, the oldest texts associated with Hinduism,1 were handed down by voice for thousands of years. UNESCO, which proclaimed the tradition of Vedic chanting in 2003 and inscribed it in 2008,2 explains how: to ensure that the sound of each word remains unaltered, practitioners are taught from childhood complex recitation techniques.3 Only thirteen of the more than one thousand Vedic recitation branches have survived.4 Some of the techniques rearrange the words. Beside the continuous text, the samhitā, students learn a word-by-word form, the pada, and patterns such as krama, in overlapping pairs,5 and jaṭā, where each pair runs forwards, backwards and forwards again.6 The krama form is about 2,500 years old.7 The scholar J. F. Staal observed that the device, begun as a means of preserving the sacred text, gradually became an end in itself.8

Here you borrow only the shape of these patterns, never a sacred text, and you use it on ordinary words.

  1. Straight through. Say the eight words in order, twice.
  2. Word by word. Each word alone, with a pause after it.
  3. Pairs. River lantern, lantern falcon, falcon copper, and on to the end.
  4. Weave. River lantern lantern river river lantern; then lantern falcon falcon lantern lantern falcon; and on.
  5. Test it cold. An hour later, say the list straight, then backwards.
Drill Run these eight everyday words through the pada, krama and jaṭā patterns, aloud. The quiz will ask for them.
  1. river
  2. lantern
  3. falcon
  4. copper
  5. meadow
  6. compass
  7. harbor
  8. saffron

Notice what the weave does. Every word is said beside its neighbors on both sides, forwards and backwards, so a dropped or swapped word stands out at once.

concepts.title: Myth check: better memories in the old days?
concepts.contentHtml:
Myth People in the ancient world and in oral cultures simply had better memories than we do.
Reality Even Yates half believed it, writing that the classical art could depend on faculties of intense visual memorization which we have lost.1 The evidence points to technique, not different brains. Lord's singers rebuilt songs from stock phrases and themes, and Vedic reciters drilled their patterns from childhood. In 2021 a Monash University team including Yunkaporta taught first-year medical students an Aboriginal narrative method. Its framing comes from Aboriginal practice: to learn new information that is not part of the songline tradition, it is common to build a story from the plants, animals and landscape of a local place. Both methods tested, this one and the memory palace, helped,2 and the Aboriginal method gave the biggest gain in the chance of perfect recall of a 20-word list.3 It was a small study of 76 students,4 and the authors put cultural safety first: the method was taught by an Aboriginal educator, with the permission of elders.

A popular theory goes further. In The Memory Code (2016) Lynne Kelly argues that many prehistoric monuments, Stonehenge among them, were built as memory spaces. Treat it as a live debate, not a finding: Publishers Weekly called the book intriguing, if not entirely persuasive, and judged that its conclusion that the method of loci is the universal driver is not supported.

Wait, really? The oldest complaint about memory technology is about writing itself. In Plato's Phaedrus, King Thamus warns the god who invented letters that the invention will produce forgetfulness in the minds of those who learn to use it, because they will not practice their memory. We know his warning only because Plato wrote it down.
